title: Question 4
stem:
A coaxial cable is frequently used to connect an aerial to a television receiver. Such a cable is illustrated in Fig. 4.1.

{{figure:figure_4_1}}

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Suggest two functions of the copper braid.
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 4.1 - there is a central copper core and an outer copper braid. For any electrical signal to flow in a complete circuit, what second path is needed?
Hint 2: Think about the TV signal travelling in the core. It is surrounded completely by the braid - how could that surrounding metal layer protect the inner signal from outside electrical noise?
parts.proper_answer: 1. Acts as the return conductor for the signal. 2. Provides shielding of the core from external noise / interference / crosstalk.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Think About the Complete Circuit**
You are sitting with the cable in front of you. The signal goes down the central copper core to the TV, but current must always have a return path to complete the loop. The outer copper braid is a good conductor that surrounds the core, so it acts as that return wire.

Step 2: **Think About Protection From Noise**
TV signals are small and at high frequency, so they are easily spoiled by stray electromagnetic waves from other wires and devices. Because the braid completely encloses the core, it acts like a metal screen. Unwanted external fields induce currents in the braid rather than in the core, so the inner signal stays clean.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Suggest two reasons why a wire pair is not usually used to connect the aerial to the receiver.

markscheme_points.text: reflections due to poor impedance matching

hints: Hint 1: A TV signal from an aerial carries a lot of information at high frequency. Compare what you know about the bandwidth and signal quality of a simple twisted wire pair with that of a coaxial cable.
Hint 2: Picture two bare wires running from the roof to the TV with no outer metal screen around them. What will happen as they pick up stray signals and lose energy along the way?
parts.proper_answer: Any two from: small bandwidth; susceptible to noise / interference / crosstalk; large attenuation / energy loss; reflections due to poor impedance matching. [Any two, 1 mark each]
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why Bandwidth Matters**
A television signal needs a wide range of high frequencies to carry picture and sound detail. A simple wire pair has only a small bandwidth, so it cannot carry this high-frequency information as well as a coaxial cable.

Step 2: **Why Noise and Loss Matter**
A wire pair has no surrounding metal shield. That means it easily picks up external noise, interference and crosstalk from other circuits, and it also radiates and loses more signal energy by attenuation. The picture at the receiver would be noisy and weak, so coaxial cable is preferred.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The coaxial cable connecting an aerial to a receiver has length $14\,\text{m}$.
The cable has an attenuation per unit length of $190\,\text{dB km}^{-1}$.

Calculate the fractional loss in signal power during transmission of the signal along the cable.
hints: Hint 1: Check the units carefully - attenuation is given as $190\text{ dB km}^{-1}$ but the cable length is only $14\text{ m}$. How will you put these into the same length unit first?
Hint 2: Recall how total attenuation in dB is linked to the ratio of output power to input power using a logarithm to base 10.
Hint 3: Once you have the total loss in dB, set up the equation to solve for the power ratio $P_{OUT}/P_{IN}$ by undoing the logarithm.
Hint 4: Remember fractional loss is not the transmitted fraction, but the fraction that is lost: $(P_{IN} - P_{OUT})/P_{IN}$. How do you get this from $P_{OUT}/P_{IN}$?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the Total Attenuation in dB**
Attenuation adds up along the length. First convert length to km: $$14\text{ m} = 14 \times 10^{-3}\text{ km}$$ Then: $$\text{attenuation} = 190 \times 14 \times 10^{-3} = 2.66\text{ dB}$$ This is the total loss in decibels from aerial to receiver.

Step 2: **Link Decibels to Power Ratio**
For power, the decibel definition is: $$\text{loss in dB} = 10 \lg\left(\frac{P_{IN}}{P_{OUT}}\right) = -10 \lg\left(\frac{P_{OUT}}{P_{IN}}\right)$$ So here: $$2.66 = -10 \lg\left(\frac{P_{OUT}}{P_{IN}}\right)$$

Step 3: **Solve for the Transmitted Fraction**
Divide by -10 and undo the log with $10^x$: $$\lg\left(\frac{P_{OUT}}{P_{IN}}\right) = -0.266$$ $$\frac{P_{OUT}}{P_{IN}} = 10^{-0.266} \approx 0.54$$ So only about 54% of the input power reaches the receiver.

Step 4: **Convert to Fractional Loss**
Fractional loss means fraction lost, not fraction received: $$\text{fractional loss} = \frac{P_{IN} - P_{OUT}}{P_{IN}} = 1 - \frac{P_{OUT}}{P_{IN}}$$ $$\text{fractional loss} = 1 - 0.54 = 0.46$$
